analysis.one_liner: Bans corporate and union campaign committees, caps their contributions, and limits congressional mass mailings.
analysis.headline: A sweeping campaign finance bill introduced by House Republican Leader Robert Michel drew no cosponsors and died in committee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would overhaul how federal campaigns are financed: it would eliminate the exception that lets corporations, labor unions, and trade associations run political action committees, cut in half what a multi-candidate PAC can give a candidate, and make it unlawful for banks, corporations, and unions to finance political committees. It would also restrict third parties from bundling employee contributions, require unions to notify workers they can opt out of paying for political activity, ban surplus campaign money from being kept or transferred to other candidates, curtail free mass mailings by members of Congress, force disclosure of party accounts spent on mixed federal-state activities, and set standards against gerrymandered congressional districts. It never got a hearing or a vote; it sat in three House committees until the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Voters would face fewer channels for corporate and union money in campaigns, and challengers would benefit from tighter contribution limits and districts not drawn to protect incumbents. Taxpayers would save on unsolicited mass franked mail, and workers could opt out of funding union political activity.

how_it_helps.text: The bill deletes the legal exception that allows corporations, labor unions, and trade associations to sponsor political action committees, and makes it unlawful for banks, corporations, and unions to fund the establishment or administration of any political committee [S2].
It cuts the cap on what a multi-candidate PAC can contribute to a candidate from $5,000 to $2,500 per election [S2].
It bars surplus campaign funds from being kept by candidates or passed to other committees; leftovers must go to retiring contributors or the national debt [S2].

It bans the congressional frank for unsolicited mass mailings and requires members to pay postage beyond a population-based allocation, with quarterly public statements of each member's mailing costs [S2].

It sets standards for drawing congressional districts — compactness, minimal splitting of counties and cities, no dilution of voting strength — and gives any eligible voter expedited access to federal court to challenge noncompliant maps [S2].
It repeals the three-year statute of limitations on campaign law violations, restoring a five-year window, and lets the FEC share compliance files with the Attorney General for investigations [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Corporations, labor unions, and trade associations lose their political committees and their ability to pool member or employee money; incumbent members of Congress lose free mass mailings and gerrymander-protected districts; and political parties gain the offsetting role of larger coordinated expenditures and unlimited transfers of campaign surpluses.

drawbacks.text: Eliminating corporate and union PACs while nearly tripling what national party committees may spend in coordinated support would concentrate campaign money in the hands of national party leadership rather than spreading it across candidates [S2].

The employee-protection provisions impose detailed notification, audit, and accounting requirements on unions for political spending funded by dues, which unions could treat as a burden on their political participation even as they protect workers who object to it [S2].

Restricting bundling through conduits and limiting intermediaries to two contributions from the same employer or union could make it harder for ordinary employees to pool small contributions for candidates they support [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core reductions in special-interest money — banning corporate and union PACs, halving PAC contribution limits, and cutting off conduit bundling — directly attack the channels that concentrated economic interests use to influence elections, and the franking and redistricting provisions curb officeholder self-protection. But the bill is not neutral in design: it shifts the freed-up money toward national party committees with much higher spending authority, which would centralize power in party leadership, and it layers compliance obligations onto unions. On balance it would materially reduce the weight of economic interests in campaigns while creating a new consolidation at the party level.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to three House committees the day it was introduced, passed along to two subcommittees within two weeks, and then sat with no hearings, no markup, and no vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Robert Michel, the House Republican leader, introduced the bill on October 5, 1989 [S1].
It was jointly referred to the House Administration, Post Office and Civil Service, and Judiciary committees on the day of introduction [S5].
Within two weeks it was referred to the Judiciary Subcommittee on Elections and the Ways and Means Subcommittee on Economic and Commercial Law [S5].
No cosponsors signed on at any point during the Congress [S4].
No further action was taken, and the bill expired when the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991 [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The existing campaign money system — corporate and union PACs, conduit bundling, and incumbents' franked-mail subsidies — was left untouched because the bill never advanced.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote and drew zero cosponsors from either party, so no recorded vote shows a partisan split; its only sponsor was the top House Republican and it died in committees run by Democrats.

industries.industry: Corporate political action committees and trade associations
industries.note: The bill eliminates the legal exception letting corporations and trade associations organize PACs and makes corporate financing of political committees unlawful. Their pooled corporate money would disappear from federal elections.

Union PACs would be banned, and unions would face detailed notification, audit, and accounting duties before spending dues money on politics; workers could reduce dues by their share of political spending. Unions and corporations lose the same funding channel.

The bill raises the coordinated spending limits for party committees from 2 to 5 cents per voter and allows unlimited transfers of candidate surpluses to parties, shifting the money freed up from PACs into party hands.

Members would lose unsolicited mass franked mail, pay postage beyond a population-based allocation, and face quarterly published statements of their mailing costs; redistricting standards and court access would make safe, gerrymandered seats harder to protect.
